note.headline: Tesla at 385.46 after an 11.46% jump with no news; margins shrinking, still avoid
note.happening: Tesla closed at 385.46, up 11.46% on the day. There is no news since the last note to explain the move. The price is now close to its 20-day average of 384.49 and above its 50-day (376.17) and 200-day (381.53) averages, but all three averages are flat and the overall trend is still marked as down. The next earnings report is due on 2027-01-27.
note.business: Today's jump changes the price, not the business. The latest filed quarter (ended 2026-09-30, filed 2026-10-22) shows that sales growth stopped. Sales were down 0.17% from a year earlier, after growing 15.78% two quarters ago. Operating margin (profit from operations per dollar of sales) fell to 3.35% from 4.74%. Free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) over the last 12 months fell to 3.3B from 6.8B. Two filing-based warnings point the same way. Inventory is up 15% while sales are up 0%, and unsold cars can force price cuts. Each dollar invested now earns 5¢ a year, down from 33¢ three years ago. At risk: margins and cash generation if inventory forces discounts. Not at risk: the balance sheet. Tesla has 37.5B of net cash (cash minus debt) and 45.4B of liquidity, so funding is not a problem. The fear in the wider tech market noted by the macro view affects sentiment only. It does not change demand or margins.
note.worth: The two valuation methods give very different answers. A discounted cash flow model (DCF: today's value of the cash the business is expected to produce) puts fair value at 20.01 to 44.3, with a base case of 24.66. That is because it starts from only 3.3B of free cash flow. Even if growth starts at 30%, the DCF value is only 44.63. Tesla's own price-to-sales history (what investors paid per dollar of sales over 5 years) gives 203.8 / 293.94 / 399.81. At 385.46 the stock is near the top of that history, in the 63rd percentile of the last 5 years, at 14.7 times sales and 424.1 times trailing earnings. The filings note that the price needs about 51% a year growth, while the business delivered 3% a year over 3 years. So the gap between the methods comes down to one choice: value Tesla on its thin current cash flow, or on what the market has historically paid for its sales. Note: the data's valuation summary still quotes a price of 345.82, which is the 2026-11-20 options-chain price from before today's jump.
bull: The balance sheet is strong. Tesla has 37.5B of net cash and 45.4B of liquidity, so it can fund heavy spending without borrowing stress.
Sales over the last 12 months still grew, to 103.6B from 95.6B (8.3%), and analysts' next-year EPS (earnings per share) growth is 25%.
